1.note: Read as "beguiled me" (as Gen 3:13 הַנָּחָשׁ הִשִּׁיאַנִי). A reading "and lifted me up", from נשׂא as in the line before, is also possible.

2.note: Shittim is the biblical place (Num 25:1). Tel Ḥittim is probably Ḥattin (Kefar Ḥittim) near Tiberias; it also sets up the rhyme with "as one beats out wheat" (חִטִּים), two lines below.

3.note: הֲדֹם is a footstool (Ps 110:1). Here it seems to mean "your house", the place where Ḥever sat at Heman's feet; the sense is uncertain.

4.note: עָשׁ is a constellation (Job 9:9), usually taken as the Great Bear. "To tread on the head of the Bear" means to be at the height of fortune.

5.note: Isa 55:13. In this poem of comfort the newborn son (the cypress) takes the place of the dead daughter (the thorn). The first half of the line runs on into the second: יִנְחֲלוּ / כָבוֹד, "shall inherit honor".

6.he: וְתַחַת אוֹר הַלְּבָנָה עָלָה אוֹר חֶרֶס
6.note: חֶרֶס is the sun (Job 9:7). The moon (feminine in Hebrew) stands for the dead daughter, the sun for the newborn son: the letter mourns and congratulates at once, as the prince asked.

7.note: This passage is missing from the Ben-Yehuda text and is taken from Kaminka's edition (Warsaw 1899, pp. 218–219), unvocalized.

8.note: Kaminka prints בארץ ("in the land"); the sense and the series of pairs need בארז, "for the cedar" (cedar and acacia together in Isa 41:19), and the translation follows that. In each pair that follows, a woman's thing (the dead daughter's) is exchanged for a man's (the newborn son's); the bier (מטה) is also a bed.
